title: Trungpa's Path of Liberation and Right Mindfulness
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up right mindfulness, the piece missing from the series on the Eightfold Path, and then turns to Chögyam Trungpa Rinpoche's book The Truth of Suffering and the Path of Liberation. After Mary Oliver's poem "The Swan," Kanho lists the four Satipatthanas (body, feelings, mind, phenomena), quotes the Buddha telling a monk that the world is whatever disintegrates, and describes mindfulness as a supervisor keeping right effort on course. Kanho names Trungpa's controversial conduct plainly, then walks through his four qualities of the path: path, insight, practice, and fruition. Kanho closes with the bodhisattva vows and a second Mary Oliver poem about saving the only life you can save.

One is another look, yet another look at right mindfulness.

Mary Oliver, "The Swan."

Did you see it in the morning rising into the silvery air?
An armful of white blossoms, a perfect commotion of silk and linen as it leaned into the bondage of its wings.

Its feet like black leaves.*
*Its wings like the stretching light of the river.

And have you changed your life?*
I chose this Mary Oliver poem, "The Swan," for the last three lines.
*And did you feel it in your heart, how it pertained to everything?
And have you, too, finally figured out what beauty is for?
And have you changed your life?*
I feel it is so fitting for our continued study of the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path.
And why?
Are you feeling it in your heart, how it pertained to everything?
And are you seeing the beauty we create when we finally figure it out, even if it is just a little bit?
And most importantly, have you decided to change your life?
As I was looking at the talks that have been given so far, I noticed that we left out right mindfulness from the Noble Eightfold Path.
So at least that's what I saw.
I could totally be wrong.
In today's language, you might find more people who are familiar with John Kabat-Zinn's definition of mindfulness.
"Mindfulness is awareness that arises through paying attention on purpose in the present moment, non-judgmentally," says John Kabat-Zinn.
And then sometimes add "in the service of self-understanding and wisdom."
Some people even believe that John Kabat-Zinn invented mindfulness.
Buddha beat him by about 2,500 years.
So, not so fast, John Kabat-Zinn.
Even though it's beautiful how much mindfulness has become a part of normal language, not something exotic or esoteric, mindfulness has always been an integral part of Buddhist practice.
And we know that predates the current mindfulness movement by quite a bit.
In Buddhist literature, there are four kinds of mindfulness.
Mindfulness in Pali is called Satipatana.
So there are four mindfulnesses or Satipatanas, and you can find them throughout the Pali canon.

Those four mindfulnesses are: mindfulness of the body, you know, body scan and knowing what's going on, where we are tied, where we are carrying a load; feelings, including emotions; mindfulness of mind; and mindfulness of phenomena or Dhammas.
Dhamma is, again, one of those technical terms.
There's a capital D, Dhamma or Dharma, which is the Buddhist teachings, the law.
So Dhammas with a small d, they're just the smallest unit of phenomenon.
Anything we see, hear, taste, touch.
If I really tried to get into this, we would be spending the next couple of months on the Satipatanas.
This is what the Buddha said about mindfulness in one of the longer discourses, [unclear: "Yannicaya"].
"And what is the faculty of Sati?"
Sati is part of the word Satipatana, the mind.
*There is the case where a disciple of the noble ones has Sati, is endowed with excellent proficiency in Sati, remembering and recollecting what was done and said a long time ago.
He remains focused on the body in and of itself, ardent, alert, and having Sati, subduing greed and distress with reference to the world.

He remains focused on feelings in and of themselves, the mind in and of itself, mental qualities in and of themselves, ardent, alert, and having Sati, subduing greed and distress with reference to the world.
This is called the faculty of Sati.*
This is being mindful.
I know I'm repeating a few times what the four foundations of mindfulness are, because if you're anything like me, I always forget what was said three lines above.
So again, mindfulness of body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
The Buddha also, and I found this really fascinating, we like to look at those old teachings as: that's it, I need to get that, once I get that, I got it.
But the Buddha puts any idea that the Eightfold Noble Path or any element of it might have permanence to rest.
A monk approaches the Buddha and asks, "The world, the world, it is said.
In what respect does the word 'world' apply?"
*The Buddha replies, "Insofar as it disintegrates, monk, it is called the world.
Now, what disintegrates?
The eye disintegrates.
Forms disintegrate.
Consciousness at the eye disintegrates.
Contact at the eye disintegrates.
And whatever there is that arises in dependence on contact at the eye, experienced as pleasure, pain, or neither, that too disintegrates.
The ear disintegrates.
Sounds disintegrate.
The nose disintegrates.
Aromas disintegrate.
The tongue disintegrates.
Tastes disintegrate.
The body disintegrates.
Tactile sensations disintegrate.
The intellect disintegrates.
Ideas disintegrate.
Consciousness at the intellect disintegrates.
Contact at the intellect disintegrates.
And whatever there is that arises in dependence on contact at the intellect, experienced as pleasure, pain, or neither pleasure nor pain, that too disintegrates.
Insofar as it disintegrates, it is called the world."*
For fellow lovers of the Pali Canon, if you want to dig a bit deeper, there is the Satipatthana Samyutta in the collective talks and other sutras in the Sutta Nipata.
Also dealing with Satipatthana, there's the Anuruddha Samyutta.
And in the Middle Length Discourses, talk number 10 is the Satipatthana Sutta, which was actually the basis of the mindfulness movement, taken up lovingly by many teachers.
Last but not least, in the longer discourses, the Digha Nikaya, number 22, it's almost the same as the one before, just with the addition of the Four Noble Truths, how they interplay.
When we consider all the elements of the mindfulness sutra, we can see that right mindfulness almost has a supervisory role in our practice.
It keeps our practice on the right path.
In right view, mindfulness recognizes the right path from the wrong path.
It also remembers to stay alert and focused to the task at hand.
It motivates right effort by remembering why the right path is worth following.
And it also notices when we wander into the thickets and brambles.
It keeps us steady with right effort of what to do.
Right mindfulness points at right effort, so our practice keeps on going.
And right effort itself expressed means that we do practice right mindfulness.
A mutual arising of effort, support, and mindfulness creates a stronger whole, all parts interwoven.
If you would like to study it, there are many excellent commentaries.
Analayo Bhikkhu wrote several of them, and Joseph Goldstein has a wonderful series of recorded talks.
You can find them as audiobooks and there's a lot of stuff on YouTube.
Now I would like to switch tracks and look at one of my favorite books about the Four Noble Truths, which was Chokyong Trungpa Rinpoche's book, *The Truth of Suffering and the Path of Liberation*.
When I started to practice, I think it was at the time the best book available that spoke of the Four Noble Truths.
And it's very interesting now that I read it again, I noticed that he was very conservative in his interpretation of the Eightfold Noble Path.
He pretty much stuck to the original Pali version of the Buddha.
Preemptively, I want to mention that I am aware of Chokyong Trungpa Rinpoche's history.
I know several people who practiced with him, and they told me of his great authenticity.
They said they never had any encounters with him where he was not fully authentic.
And I respect that this is how they hold their root teacher.
I will leave it up to you how you will consider his great, deep knowledge, but also his wildness, his crazy wisdom teachings.
Trungpa was a man who contained multitudes and emptiness.
He was a supreme abbot of the Surmang monasteries, scholar, teacher, poet, artist.
He originated a radical re-presenting of Tibetan Buddhism in the West.

Some of his ways of teaching, his heavy drinking, sexual relations with his own students, and the physical assault of a student, and his wife doing some unpleasant stuff to an innocent dog, and so on, caused great controversy.
But I will let you see how you hold the totality of this teacher.
I'm not asking that we are blind to his conduct.
However, we may be opening up ourselves to great compassion.
He was human, he had flaws, and he was a teacher.
I will lean only briefly into two chapters, the sequence of the path and the four qualities of the path.
And again, I found that he was leaning quite a bit into the ancient roots of Buddhism.
Trungpa calls this stage the sequence of the path.
And I actually think "sequence of the past," yeah, it's a good way.
I might have said, where do we start?
And in this whole discussion, let us not forget Bodhicitta, our own great desire to awaken for the benefit of others.
We want to awaken the spontaneous wish and the compassionate mind to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all.
The end of suffering.
So let's say that we have learned about the Four Noble Truths and we truly accept the Four Noble Truths as a guide for ourselves, for living by vow.
And during our studies and our practice, we are guaranteed to meet challenges.
If you are living your life and you have lived your life without encountering challenges, please let me know afterwards.
I really want to talk to you.
So, challenges.
Overcoming the notion of eternity through the wisdom of impermanence is the non-theistic path of Buddhadharma.
Overcoming the search for pleasure and the avoidance of discomfort.
A little voice tries to tell me to search pleasure and distraction.
They're so much nicer than a deep dive into my real problems, into my real life.
It's important for me to remember that all distractions are impermanent.
It's like included in the word, but especially in my mind, when I lose track of things, it likes to wander into the safe space of distraction.
Let us realize the possibility of emptiness for ourselves.
Not that we go there and we live there for the rest of our life, but to visit and to understand what we saw.

Both eternalism, having some kind of eternal life as a spirit or a soul, and nihilism, that nothing really matters because we appreciate everything as oneness, as a form of emptiness, are basically just ways of reinforcing our ego.

Mindfulness, meditative awareness, and the experience of the gap between individual thoughts and actions are direct personal experiences, forging the path of our practice, keeping us free of the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.
And then, of course, encountering egolessness.
Let me read you a brief passage.
*Having realized emptiness, you also begin to realize that there is no one to hang on to that realization or to celebrate that experience.
You encounter egolessness.
Ego refers to the notion of self, that we always feel the self, the sense of center.
Centering has become a popular concept in the jargon of spirituality, but there is no mention of giving up or surrendering.
It is more like having a little doggie bag inside you to hold your leftovers.
The problem with centering is that you are coming back to a sense of your individual being as opposed to a selfless center.
A center that is very full, definite, solid, and concretized.
In that way, it's called ego.
Having such a solid sense of isness, you no longer have a path.
On the other hand, having such a problem means that you have something to work on.*
I remember at Tassajara, whenever something went wrong, there was a big problem, it was almost guaranteed that someone would come up and say, "It's good for your practice."
So the last thing I wanted to bring up was what Trungpa Rinpoche called the qualities of the path: path, insight.
So it's the path inside practice and fruition.
The first quality of path is the path.
It is interesting that Trungpa lists path as the first quality of the path.
It struck me as a little bit extra redundancy, but it is the path of insight, realizing the real meaning of dharma and the practice of suchness.
The path is rediscovering our own Buddha nature, rediscovering the Buddha nature of all you encounter.
Suchness is dropping our veils, seeing into reality itself.
The second quality of the path is insight.
We gain this insight through our daily sitting practice and through the experience of our living.
Through meditation, we find clarity in the skill and ability to fully relate to happenings without filters, without falling into the pit dug by our conditioning.
This is the appropriate response of Zen practice.
Our habit energy is clearly visible at this point, giving us the opportunity to clarify our mind and remove hindrances or obstacles.
The third quality of path is practice.
Chokyam Trungpa Rinpoche puts it like this: associating with basic sanity.
Our meditation practice is a different approach to life.
No judgment, no gaining idea, not figuring something out, but a slow peeling away of layers that accumulated during our long lives.
Even if for a moment we feel that we are controlling our life, reality will roll around sooner or later and remind us that it ain't so.
There is always a reminder that this illusion of control is just that, an illusion.
In meditation, we can open the hand of thought and the desire to control what we cannot control anyway, and we can just be.
The fourth quality of the path is fruition.
If we were followers of a Theravadan tradition, the ultimate fruition is permanent nirvana.
I, however, would say this.
For us, it might mean that we have found our bodhisattva path, and as it looked like, we will continue to make mistakes.
Nevertheless, we will find our way back and continue to crawl, climb, and stumble along.
The path itself becomes a treasure.
Our path points to the bodhisattva ideal, our beloved, absolutely impossible bodhisattva vows that we take over and over again.
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
For us, it's bodhisattvas in the making.
The fruition may be to achieve enlightenment and to fulfill the vow to become a Buddha.
But don't forget, the bodhisattva forgoes entrance into permanent nirvana in order to remain in this world as a guide and helper for all those beings we vow to save.
I hope that pulling back and seeing the path from Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche's perspective has been useful.
If it has not, please forget every single word I said tonight and carry on with your practice.
Or maybe just enjoy Mary Oliver's poem, "The Journey."
*One day you finally knew what you had to do and began, though the voices around you kept shouting their bad advice.
Though the whole house began to tremble and you felt the old tug at your ankles.
"Mend my life," each voice cried.
But you didn't stop, you knew what you had to do, though the wind pried with its stiff fingers at the very foundations, though their melancholy was terrible.
It was already late enough and a wild night and a road full of fallen branches and stones.
But little by little, as you left their voices behind, the stars began to burn through the sheets of clouds.

And there was a new voice, which you slowly recognized as your own, that kept you company as you strode deeper and deeper into the world, determined to do the only thing you could do, determined to save the only life you could save.*
Thank you so much for listening.
Thank you for listening.
And maybe you could turn off the recording.
We still have a little bit of time to...

as a guide and helper for all those beings we vow to save. I hope that pulling back and seeing the path from Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche's perspective has been useful. If it has not, please forget every single word I said tonight and carry on with your practice. Or maybe just enjoy Mary Oliver's poem, The Journey. One day you finally knew what you had to do and began, though the voices around you kept shouting their bad advice.

Though the whole house began to tremble and you felt the old tug at your ankles. Meant my life, each voice cried. But you didn't stop, you knew what you had to do, though the wind pried with its stiff fingers at the very foundations, though their melancholy was terrible. It was already late enough and a wild night and a road full of fallen branches and stones.

But little by little, as you left their voices behind, the stars began to burn through the sheets of clouds. And there was a new voice, which you slowly recognized as your own, that kept you company as you strode deeper and deeper into the world, determined to do the only thing you could do, determined to save the only life you could save.
